name: Microneedling (SkinPen)

lead: SkinPen is an electric microneedling device used by clinicians for acne scars, wrinkles and overall skin texture, for smoother skin and softer scars.

Tiny punctures are thought to trigger skin repair and collagen remodelling, which is the standard description of microneedling. Registered SkinPen trials cover neck wrinkles, acne scars on the face and back, acne, hand aging and vitiligo; no results were summarised in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is done in a clinic in a series of sessions, sometimes combined with platelet-rich plasma. Results build gradually as skin remodels.
Infection is a documented risk in untrained or non-sterile settings, including a 2024 CDC report tied to a spa facial procedure. It is commonly described as FDA-cleared when used by clinicians.

angle.text: It is used for acne scars, wrinkles and overall texture: tiny punctures trigger repair and collagen remodelling, leading to smoother skin and softer scars. It is sometimes combined with platelet-rich plasma, and several small SkinPen trials are registered.

lead: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, skin needling or dermarolling, is a cosmetic procedure in which tiny sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin; SkinPen is a branded electric microneedling device used in registered clinical trials.[1] It has been used for scarring and acne, and is combined in some practices with platelet-rich plasma.[1]

Registered SkinPen trials cover wrinkles of the neck, acne scars on the face and back, acne vulgaris, hand aging and vitiligo.[2][3][4][5][6] No results from these registrations are summarised in the sources reviewed here.
The sources reviewed do not describe the device history or its regulatory clearance, although it is commonly described as FDA-cleared.
infobox: Wrinkles, acne scars, acne, hand aging, vitiligo

paras: Registered, completed studies of SkinPen include neck wrinkles (35 participants),[2] acne scars on the face or back (41),[3] facial acne vulgaris as a proof of concept (31),[4] hand aging (18),[5] and microneedling as a stand-alone vitiligo treatment (13).[6] A hand aging study was withdrawn,[7] and a study of microneedling for dermatoporosis is also registered.[8] Other registered work compares microneedling with fractional laser or with platelet-rich plasma.[9][10] Wikipedia states that some studies found adding microneedling to minoxidil more effective for hair loss than minoxidil alone, and that research on scars and acne is ongoing.[1]

Wikipedia notes infection concerns when procedures are performed by untrained people in non-medical settings, and describes an April 2024 CDC report of three women diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials at a New Mexico spa.[1]
